title: College Football: UNH falls to Merrimack, now 2-7 on season - Yahoo Sports
content: NORTH ANDOVER, Mass. – Ryan Ricketti caught 11 passes for 155 yards, but the University of New Hampshire football team lost to Merrimack College, 27-24 on Saturday, Oct. 24 in a non-conference game at Duane Stadium. The 11 receptions and 155 receiving yards were both career highs for Ricketti, who accounted for nearly half of UNH's passing offense. UNH is now 2-7 on the season. The Wildcats are off next week, and will host Rhode Island on Saturday, Nov. 7. UNH's Tommy McLeish, making his first career start at quarterback, completed 27 of 44 passes for 318 yards and two touchdowns. He was sacked three times and threw one interception. Jackson Stone recorded a team-high 10 tackles for the Wildcats, while Trevor Barry and Cohen Cook both had eight. Merrimack quarterback AJ Hairston threw for 205 yards and a touchdown while also rushing for 37 yards and two scores. His 8-yard touchdown run midway through the fourth quarter proved to be the game-winner. Merrimack is now 3-5. title: Chris Pappas Visits UNH, and Encourages Students to Vote Ahead of November Election - The New Hampshire
content: DURHAM, N.H. – U.S. Rep. Chris Pappas, D-N.H., visited the University of New Hampshire on Tuesday, Oct. 20, encouraging students to register to vote and discussing issues affecting younger generations ahead of the Nov. 3 general election. During his visit, Pappas walked through the Memorial Union Building (MUB), speaking with students about the upcoming election and the importance of political participation. He also stopped by the UNH Student Senate room, where he spoke with student representatives. Pappas, who currently represents New Hampshire's 1st Congressional District, is running for the U.S. Senate against Republican John E. Sununu. With Election Day just two weeks away, Pappas emphasized the importance of engaging younger voters and ensuring their concerns are represented in Washington. When asked why he chose to visit UNH, Pappas said he wanted to support voter registration efforts and encourage students to participate in the upcoming election. "We want to support the effort, you know, in terms of making sure people register, and have their voices heard in November," Pappas said. "It's a great campus." Throughout his visit, Pappas spoke about the role younger generations play in shaping the country's political future, arguing that students should not wait until later in life to become involved in politics. "There are people counting your generation out, people that are just trying to protect things the way that they are right now," Pappas said. Pappas argued that the current economic and political system benefits wealthy Americans and large corporations while leaving younger generations to deal with rising costs and financial uncertainty. "The status quo is working well for the corporation, for the wealthiest Americans. But what about the things that are falling on your shoulders in terms of how this economy isn't functioning, issues like housing and higher education affordability," Pappas said. Pappas encouraged students to recognize their ability to influence political decisions, particularly on issues that will affect their futures. "I’ve got to make sure that you all feel empowered to have your voice heard and sort of take control of our democracy," Pappas said. "We can't wait 20 or 30 years for that to happen. It needs to happen now." Beyond voter participation, Pappas addressed the financial challenges facing college students in New Hampshire, including the cost of higher education, housing and everyday expenses. When asked what he believes is the biggest concern facing college students in New Hampshire and how he would address it if elected to the Senate, Pappas pointed to affordability as a major issue. "The cost of everything's way too high, and whether that is tuition, housing, or just everything people need in their day-to-day lives, it's been going up over the last couple years," Pappas said. He emphasized the need for greater investment in education at both the state and federal levels, arguing that students should not have to carry the financial burden of rising costs without additional support. "UNH is last in the nation in terms of state support for education. So we’ve got to do better at the state level and the federal level too," Pappas said. He also discussed the need to lower the cost of gas, health care and housing, connecting these concerns to broader political issues in Washington. "We have to bring down the cost of gas and healthcare and housing, all the things that people need to live successful lives," Pappas said. Pappas criticized the current administration and what he described as a lack of accountability in Washington, arguing that changes in congressional leadership are necessary to address everyday concerns. "I'm really worried about where we are as a country. We've got no checks and balances in Washington right now, and a president that is totally incompetent every day," Pappas said. "So we got to stand up and demand better, and restore an ability to get things done and focus on people's day-to-day lives." When asked what sets him apart from his Republican opponent, former U.S. Sen. John E. Sununu, particularly when it comes to representing younger generations, Pappas pointed to Sununu's previous record in Washington. "He went to Washington 30 years ago. He has been a congressman, he's been a senator before," Pappas said. Pappas criticized Sununu's positions on reproductive rights, Social Security and the invasion in Iraq arguing that New Hampshire should not return to what he described as a failed political history. "That's part of a failed political history that we shouldn't have to go back to," Pappas said. "This should be about how we write a different chapter for the future." Pappas contrasted Sununu's record with his own experience representing New Hampshire and his priorities if elected to the Senate. "I have a small business background. I've been fighting hard the last few years to expand access to healthcare, to protect our environment, to protect reproductive freedom, to make sure that we're investing in education," Pappas said. "Those are fights that I want to take to the Senate." He argued that the election represents a choice between maintaining the current direction of the federal government and changing the balance of power in Washington. "I'm on the side of shaking up the status quo and making our political system function for everyday Americans and Granite Staters," Pappas said. With Election Day approaching, Pappas also shared his message for voters who remain undecided. "This is an election where we can deliver change if people are willing to speak out," Pappas said. He pointed to political dysfunction, economic inequality and the influence of wealthy individuals and corporations as reasons voters should become involved. "It doesn't have to be this way, and if people of good conscience get engaged and decide to vote, we can take the power of our democracy in our own hands," Pappas said. Pappas emphasized the importance of restoring checks and balances in Washington and changing the balance of power in the Senate. "We need to restore checks and balances in Washington and flip the majority in the U.S. Senate, so that we have some guardrails for the American people, and that we can get back down to business to solve problems again," Pappas said. He added that representing New Hampshire should involve addressing the needs of people across different generations, including students, families and older residents. "New Hampshire's a great state, there's a lot going for us. There are challenges here, and this should be about how we focus on the needs of students and families and seniors, and, you know, just make sure that everyone's heard," Pappas said. While much of his visit focused on the upcoming election, Pappas stressed that political engagement should continue beyond November. "It's not about just winning one election. It's how you build progress over time," Pappas said. "Because there are no permanent victories or defeats in our political system. You gotta keep people engaged."

title: Durham Reacts to Two New Restaurant Chains - The New Hampshire
content: DURHAM — On Sept. 23, Chipotle Mexican Grill officially opened its doors at 7 Mill Road in Durham, New Hampshire, marking the second national restaurant chain to make its local debut. Next door, Jersey Mike’s is approaching its third month of business in Durham. The arrival of both chains has generated excitement among UNH students, who now have two new dining options and potential employers close to campus. “I was really excited for the two new stores to open when I heard about it. I’m a big fan of Chipotle, and I am excited to go in Durham,” said James Reda, a senior at UNH, describing his initial reaction to the restaurants’ arrival. These new Durham locations will affect more than UNH students. Their arrival raises questions about competition, convenience and employment in a college town where local restaurants have long been part of the community. “The general consensus that we’ve heard from other business owners is that Durham had really resisted this type of business for a long time, and so a lot of people were really disappointed,” said Erin McGinley, co-owner of JP’s Grill. McGinley and her husband, Michael, bought JP’s Grill in 2018. Since then, the restaurant has become a downtown dining staple for students and residents alike. “I’d be lying if I said we weren’t disappointed,” McGinley said, describing the restaurant’s initial reaction to news of the new chains. McGinley said larger companies have a potential advantage when it comes to marketing and advertising, resources that smaller businesses often struggle to match. “You’re not going to see a JP’s logo on the ice rink, for example,” McGinley said. Like McGinley, Kim Clark, owner of Clark’s American Bistro on Main Street in Durham, shares concerns about the marketing capabilities of larger chains. Clark’s has been a family-owned establishment for over 100 years. “We are hopeful that the local community will still be interested in conducting dine and donate with us, but do wonder if their [Chipotle and Jersey Mike's] ability to market at a corporate level may impact this,” Clark said. Clark was referring to her restaurant’s weekly Dine and Donate/We Care Wednesdays, where 10% of food sales are donated to a local cause. She is also the director of business of practice and a lecturer of management at UNH. Across the street from JP’s Grill and Clark’s American Bistro, Pauly’s Pockets has also been family-owned for over 20 years right here in Durham. “This business, Mom and Pop, it’s gonna die, sooner or later,” said Paul Eja, owner of Pauly’s Pockets. “It’s a good business to be in a college town, but not like how it used to be,” Eja said. Eja sees several benefits to operating a business in a college town, including new students arriving each year, extra-busy semester periods and proximity to campus. However, he also pointed to some of the downsides of running a business in Durham. “We used to do business from 9 o’clock in the morning, the next day 3-4 o’clock in the morning. Nonstop. Then the new dining hall came onboard, and took a lot of business from Main Street,” Eja said. Like McGinley and Clark, Eja believes the new restaurants will benefit the community, even as they bring more competition to local businesses. “Good for Durham, good for students, I’m not against it, but it will take more business,” Eja said. While small businesses prepare to compete with the new establishments, students have already started digging in, and some are cashing in. “So far it has been good, I like my coworkers, everyone who works there goes to UNH so it’s been fun,” said Bella Esposito, a junior at UNH who has worked at Chipotle since its opening on September 23. Esposito has found that the majority of Chipotle’s customers are students, and lots of them. “There’s been a lot of people, and there have been days where we ran out of stuff. I worked the last tailgate and it was crazy,” Esposito said. The buzz around campus is real, as students routinely trek down to Mast Road to indulge in Durham’s latest offerings. “Only time will tell,” McGinley said, reflecting on the future of Durham’s local restaurant scene as Chipotle and Jersey Mike’s establish themselves in town.
